To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) pigeons will attack a target when given the opportunity to do so and that (2) pigeons will drink from a water spout when given the opportunity.
pigeons will attack a conspecific target on a response-independent food schedule and that attack is not suppressed by access to food.

(1) pigeons attack conspecific targets during interfood intervals on fixed-time schedules; (2) pigeons drink on fixed-time schedules, but drinking occurs less frequently and for shorter periods than attack; and (3) pigeons attack and drink more on fixed-time schedules than on a no-food baseline and attack and drink less on fixed-time schedules relative to a food baseline.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the assessment of drinking behavior in White King pigeions on response-independent schedules.
the assessment of schedules-induced drinking and aggression in pigeons.
the effects of response-independent schedules of food delivery on attack and drinking in a species that typically exhibits these behaviors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
attack is a more robust and stable response to be induced and maintained by a response-independent food schedule than drinking.
the schedule of food delivery enhanced attack and drinking, and that the effect of the food baseline was to increase attack and drinking over the no-food baseline.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
attack and drinking were induced by the fixed-time food schedule, and the schedule enhanced attack and water ingestion relative to food baselines.
attack and drinking are both sensitive to the schedule and that the food baseline may be more effective than the no-food one for assessing the schedule effects on drinking and attack.
attack and drinking are both enhanced by response-independent food delivery and are positively correlated with each other.

the fixed-time schedule of food delivery, in combination with access to a conspecific target and water, results in a high rate of attack and water ingestion in White King pigeoms.
attack and drinking can be assessed in the same experiment using a single food schedule and that attack and drinking are enhanced by the schedule.
